LESSON 88 OF 106·Offensive Thinking and Safe Testing

From Finding to Fixing: Writing a Usable Report

Why a report is a work order rather than a trophy: the five layers a finding needs, the decisions that stay with the organisation, and the question that makes the next one cheaper.

Applied Foundation2 min
Why this matters

A finding nobody can act on is a finding that will not be fixed. The report is the deliverable, and its quality matters more than the sophistication of how the issue was found.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Interactive mental model for From Finding to Fixing: Writing a Usable Report: compare normal operation, boundary failure, and defensive design.

03 Protected State
  1. Source: A usable finding states the impact in the owner terms, not in the researcher technique.
  2. Boundary: The system processes well-formed input along the intended happy path.
  3. Outcome: State transitions and responses remain within expected operational bounds.
01 Untrusted Input
Tampered state
02 Unchecked Assumption
Unblocked
03 Boundary Bypass
  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check whether every finding has reproducible steps that a sceptical person can follow.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input
Enforced control
02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Track findings in one place with an owner and a due date, and review open ones regularly.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • check whether every finding has reproducible steps that a sceptical person can follow
  • check whether impact is stated in business terms rather than only in technical ones
  • check whether the recommendation is specific enough to be turned into a change
  • check whether the severity reflects this environment exposure, not just the issue in the abstract

How it works

  • A usable finding states the impact in the owner terms, not in the researcher technique.
  • Reproduction has to be reliable and quick, because the first person to verify it decides whether it gets fixed.
  • Evidence should show the problem occurred, not merely that a scanner thought it might.
  • A specific remediation is worth more than a general principle, because the owner has to decide what to change.
  • Severity should be argued from impact and exposure, and the argument should be visible in the report.

The background

  • Early penetration test reports were long narratives, which read well and changed very little.
  • Standardised report formats emerged so that findings could be tracked to closure across teams.
  • The industry moved toward a common weakness classification, which made severity comparable between tools and reports.
  • Bug bounty platforms imposed short structured templates, which is why most modern reports are structured.

Real-world examples

  • A report with twenty pages of narrative and no reproduction steps gets closed as unverifiable.
  • A one-page report with a clear impact statement and a specific fix gets fixed.
  • A severity argument based on scanner rating alone is easily overruled by a team that knows their own exposure.

What to look for

  • Check whether every finding has reproducible steps that a sceptical person can follow.
  • Check whether impact is stated in business terms rather than only in technical ones.
  • Check whether the recommendation is specific enough to be turned into a change.
  • Check whether the severity reflects this environment exposure, not just the issue in the abstract.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Track findings in one place with an owner and a due date, and review open ones regularly.
  • Retest what you fixed and close on evidence rather than on the developer word.
  • Write the report so a busy person can act in five minutes: summary, impact, reproduction, fix.
  • Feed recurring findings back into code review and pipeline checks so the category does not return.
  • Accept that not everything gets fixed, and record the accepted risk explicitly rather than silently.
